title: Inferring Acceptance and Rejection in Dialogue by Default Rules of Inference
research_question: How can conversational participants infer acceptance or rejection of assertions and proposals when responses are indirect, logically consistent with what they reject, or only partially accept the preceding propositional content?
methodology: The paper combines corpus analysis, discourse/pragmatic analysis, prosodic analysis, and formal modeling. Walker examines a five-hour corpus of 55 live financial-advice dialogues, supplemented with examples from the literature, identifying 43 acceptance examples and 31 rejection examples; she also defines informationally redundant utterances (IRUs) and codes 184 IRUs for factors including logical relation, antecedent distance, speaker relation, phrase-final tone, and intonational contour. Distributional and prosodic patterns are analyzed, including a reported chi-square test, and naturally occurring examples are used to develop a taxonomy of rejection. The empirical observations are then incorporated into a default-inference model of common ground that distinguishes hypotheses, defaults, and more strongly supported propositions.

key_findings.finding: Logical consistency is necessary but not sufficient for interpreting a response as acceptance, while logical inconsistency is sufficient but not necessary for interpreting a response as rejection.
A reply can accept an entailed subproposition of a preceding assertion while rejecting the stronger assertion, so acceptance and rejection scope can differ within the same antecedent proposition.
key_findings.section: 1 Introduction; 5 Adding to the Common Ground; 6 Discussion of Open Issues and Future Work

key_findings.finding: The corpus analysis motivates three rejection classes beyond straightforward denial, contradiction, and refusal: implicature rejections, epistemic rejections, and deliberation rejections.
A less informative reply can reject only the omitted or replaced portion of a stronger antecedent through scalar implicature rather than rejecting every proposition entailed by the antecedent.
key_findings.section: 3.1.1 Rejection by Implicature; 6 Discussion of Open Issues and Future Work

key_findings.finding: Information structure and prosody help distinguish a partial repetition functioning as acceptance from a superficially similar logically consistent utterance functioning as rejection; acceptances tend to re-realize focal material as old information, whereas implicature rejections substitute a scalarly related focal item.
key_findings.section: 2.2 Distributional Analysis of Acceptances; 4 The Role of Information Structure in distinguishing Acceptance and Implicature Rejection; 7 Conclusion

key_findings.finding: IRUs may have more than one discourse antecedent; the paper notes examples where a response depends on two preceding utterances, although its corpus coding operationally treats the most recent utterance as the IRU antecedent in such cases.

The proposed common-ground model represents partial acceptance by adding the proposition explicitly realized by the response while allowing a default rejection inference to defeat acceptance of the stronger antecedent.
key_findings.section: 5 Adding to the Common Ground; 6 Discussion of Open Issues and Future Work

key_findings.finding: Fall-Rise intonation can assist in identifying rejection, but it is neither necessary nor sufficient for rejection by itself.
key_findings.section: 4.2 Fall-Rise as an Indicator of Rejection

limitations: The empirical corpus is small and domain-specific: 55 financial-advice dialogues comprising about five hours of speech.
Only 31 rejection instances were identified in the 55 dialogues, including 19 rejections of assertions and 12 rejections of proposals.
Acceptance and rejection classifications were based on the author's interpretations; no independent annotation or inter-annotator agreement is reported.
The author explicitly states that the proposed classification should be tested on a larger corpus with speech available.
Explicit forms such as direct yes/agreement and no/refusal are deliberately excluded from much of the linguistic-cue analysis.
The adequacy of the formal representation of partial acceptance remains an open issue; the paper discusses alternative modifications but does not resolve them.

Although multiple antecedents are acknowledged, the operational corpus treatment chooses the most recent utterance as the antecedent, so genuinely multi-antecedent response-link representation is not developed.
No systematic treatment of multi-question antecedents or unanswered subquestions is provided.
raw_claims: Responses that are logically consistent with an antecedent can nevertheless function as rejections.
A response may accept a weaker proposition entailed by an antecedent while rejecting the antecedent's stronger content.
The financial-advice corpus contains substantially fewer rejection examples than acceptance-related material.
Rejections of assertions and rejections of proposals require partly different kinds of inference.
Scalar implicature can make an informationally weaker response reject a stronger preceding assertion.
Epistemic rejection can arise from default reasoning about another speaker's beliefs rather than direct contradiction of uttered content.
Deliberation rejection can arise from reasoning about intentions, alternatives, consequences, and the desirability of proposed actions.
Adjacent informationally redundant utterances by the other speaker occupy a position associated with expression of attitude toward the prior contribution.
Some informationally redundant responses have multiple preceding utterances contributing antecedent content.
Prosodic realization provides evidence for distinguishing acceptance functions from other uses of informationally redundant utterances.
Fall-Rise intonation is a useful but non-determinative cue to rejection.
The proposed common-ground representation keeps acceptance defeasible long enough for conflicting default rejection inferences to override it.
